meta.title: The Word on the Board
meta.skill_frame: Literary text: notice a detail the story repeats and what the repeat means.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a third-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured FK 4.27 and 3.55 on the two parts (53 and 47 words), 3.92 together. The load is one repeated word and one pass, so the reader tracks a single clue twice. That sits inside the grade 2-3 band and below the 4.1 floor, which measures 5.3 at its easiest.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.attribution: Original text drafted for literary_text 3.1, band 3.1, sequence 4. No external work.
source.text_status: Drafted for the band, accepted on spot check.
source.survey: A coach who writes the same word before and after a game, built so the repeated word carries the change in the youngest player.
source.avoided: No team name, league, or score. No claim about the other team.

session.difficulty_basis: One word repeated before and after the game, and the second use carries the meaning.

authoring_exceptions: Parts run 45-60 words instead of 100-200. At band 3.1 the text is short by design: two parts keep the session inside 12 minutes and the whole story stays visible on one screen. Recorded under 2.1.

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: The team trains on the same field every week, whatever the weather. Before each game the coach writes one word on the board in the changing room: look. The players laugh about it, but the word stays up. The youngest player is the fastest on the team, and she never passes the ball.
passage.part_2: In the last minute she takes the ball down the wing with two players closing on her. She looks up, sees a teammate alone in front of the goal, and passes. The teammate scores. After the game the coach writes the same word on the board again.

items.prompt: What word does the coach write on the board?

tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage says the coach writes one word on the board: look.
tutor_only.tell: The coach writes the word look on the board before each game.
help: The sentence about the board names the word.
It is a short word about where the eyes go.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.ask: Passing is what the player does at the end. What word does the coach write?

items.prompt: The youngest player is the fastest on the team. What does she never do?

tutor_only.confirm: Yes. She never passes the ball.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage says she is the fastest and she never passes the ball.
tutor_only.tell: She is the fastest player, and she never passes the ball.
help: The sentence about the youngest player gives both facts.
One fact is about speed, and the other is about the ball.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says she never scores
if_they_say.ask: The passage does not mention her scoring. What does it say she never does with the ball?

items.prompt: She looks up before she passes. Why does that matter?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. Looking up lets her see the teammate alone in front of the goal.
tutor_only.correct_reason: She looks up, sees a teammate alone in front of the goal, and passes.
tutor_only.tell: Looking up is what shows her the teammate alone in front of the goal.
help: Look at what she sees after she looks up.
The sentence names a teammate and the goal.
tutor_only.core_idea: She sees the teammate alone in front of the goal.
accept_ideas: she spots the teammate in front of the goal
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says she looks at the crowd
if_they_say.ask: The passage says she sees a teammate. What is that teammate doing?

items.prompt: The coach writes the same word after the team wins. Why write it again?

tutor_only.confirm: Yes. The word worked, and he wants it to stay.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The pass that won the game came after she looked up, so the coach writes the word again.
tutor_only.tell: The word won the game. The coach writes it again so the players keep looking up.
help: Compare the board before the game with the board after it.
The word did its work in the last minute.
tutor_only.core_idea: Because looking up won the game, and he wants them to keep doing it.
accept_ideas: to remind them to keep looking
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says the players forgot the word
if_they_say.ask: The word was on the board before the game. Why write it after a win?

items.prompt: The story shows a fast player and one word on a board. What does it show about being fast?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. Being fast is not enough on its own.
tutor_only.correct_reason: She is the fastest player and never passes, and the goal comes only after she looks up and passes.
tutor_only.tell: Speed alone did not score the goal. She scored it after she looked up and passed.
help: Look at what she does before the pass.
She is fast all game, and the goal comes after she looks up.
tutor_only.core_idea: Being fast is not enough without looking up.
accept_ideas: fast players still need to pass
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says fast players always score
if_they_say.ask: The passage says she is the fastest and she never passes. What happens when she looks up?
